title: Comparison Operators
description: Asking questions that produce true or false, and why text needs equals rather than ==.

content.value: Questions with a Yes or No Answer
Arithmetic gives a number. A **comparison** gives a `boolean`: `true` or `false`, nothing else. It is how a program asks about its own values.

content.text: It weighs two values and gives one answer: yes (`true`) or no (`false`).

items.sub: greater or equal, less or equal

content.caption: These six operators are what Module 4 is built on: a decision is a comparison plus something to do about the answer.

content.question: What does `System.out.println(8 >= 8);` print?
content.explain: `>=` means greater than **or equal to**, and 8 is equal to 8.

steps.note: Two `==`: ask "is it 1?" Yes. Nothing changes.

content.title: Watch = and == at work
content.outro: Writing `=` where you meant `==` is usually a compile error in Java, because an assignment is not a boolean.

content.question: Which line checks whether `lives` is 0?
content.explain: Two equals signs ask a question. One equals sign would store 0.

parts.label: name
parts.note: A name that says what the answer means.

content.title: A comparison stored in a boolean
content.caption: Name the answer once and reuse it: `passed` explains itself.
Sample run: type `75` and it prints `Passed:  true` then `Perfect: false`.

content.question: What is stored in `passed`?
content.explain: 50 is not **greater** than 50, so `score > 50` is `false`. `>=` would have given `true`.

content.value: For text, `==` checks whether two values are the very same object in memory, not whether they spell the same thing. Use `.equals(...)` to compare the letters.

items.title: Unreliable
items.text: Typed text is a fresh object, so this can be `false` even when the letters match. No error warns you.

items.title: Correct
items.text: Compares the characters. Gives a `boolean` like any comparison.

content.caption: Text written directly in code shares one copy, so `==` can look right by luck. Use `.equals` for text, every time.

content.value: `equalsIgnoreCase` works like `equals` but treats `Yes`, `YES` and `yes` as the same. Often what you want for typed answers.
Decimals are not stored exactly, so two sums that should agree can differ in the last digit. Use `<` and `>` freely on doubles, but be careful with `==`.

content.caption: Nothing is broken. Real programs check that the difference between two decimals is tiny instead of asking for an exact match.

items.title: Compile error
items.text: Text and a number: Java refuses to guess what this means.

items.title: Parse first
items.text: Turn the text into an `int`, then compare. Gives `true`.

content.question: Which line safely checks if the String `name` is `"Sam"`?
content.explain: `.equals` compares the letters. `==` on text can give the wrong answer without any error.

practice.question: Store two ages in `int` variables. Print whether the first is older, whether they are the same age, and whether they are different.
Ask for a password with `nextLine()` and print whether it equals `pocketlab`, using the right method for comparing text.
Ask for a temperature and store two booleans: whether it is above 35, and whether it is below 10. Print both with labels.

quiz.question: What type does a comparison like `score > 50` produce?
quiz.explain: Every comparison produces `true` or `false`, which is exactly what a `boolean` holds. That is why you can store one in a boolean variable.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
options: `=` stores a value; `==` asks whether two values are equal.
They are the same, but `==` is clearer.
quiz.explain: One equals sign assigns. Two equals signs compare and produce a boolean. Mixing them up is the classic beginner bug.

quiz.question: A person typed `yes` into a Scanner, stored as `answer`. What does `answer == "yes"` give?
options: false, because == compares objects rather than characters
quiz.explain: Text from a Scanner is a new object, so `==` says false even though the letters match. `answer.equals("yes")` asks the right question.

quiz.question: Which is the right way to check that a String called `name` holds `Amara`?
quiz.explain: `.equals` compares the characters. `==` compares objects, and a single `=` would overwrite the variable instead of asking anything.

quiz.question: Why does `(0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3` give false?
options: Doubles are not stored exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004.
You cannot use == on doubles at all.
Java rounds all doubles to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Binary fractions cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so the sum is a hair away from 0.3. Use `<` and `>` freely, and be careful with `==` on decimals.

quiz.question: Why is `"10" > 5` a compile error?
options: One side is text, and Java will not compare unrelated types.
quiz.explain: Java refuses to guess what comparing text to a number should mean. Parse the text with `Integer.parseInt` first, then compare two numbers.
